entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen10085" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10086" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10087" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10087" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10086" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10088" type="x-p"/> Samuel sends Saul to destroy the Amalekites, and all their substance, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.3">1Sam 15:1-3</reference>. Saul collects an immense army and comes against their city, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.4">1Sam 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.5">1Sam 15:5</reference>. He desires the Kenites to remove from among the Amalekites, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.6">1Sam 15:6</reference>. He smites the Amalekites, and takes their king, Agag, prisoner, and saves the best of the spoil, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.7-1Sam.15.9">1Sam 15:7-9</reference>. The Lord is displeased, and sends Samuel to reprove him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.10">1Sam 15:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.11">1Sam 15:11</reference>. The conversation between Samuel and Saul, in which the latter endeavors to justify his conduct, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.12-1Sam.15.23">1Sam 15:12-23</reference>. He is convinced that he has done wrong, and asks pardon, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.24-1Sam.15.31">1Sam 15:24-31</reference>. Samuel causes Agag to be slain; for which he assigns the reasons, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.32-1Sam.15.35">1Sam 15:32-35</reference>. <div eID="gen10088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10089" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10090" type="x-p"/> The Lord sent me to anoint thee - This gave him a right to say what immediately follows.
entries.content_plain:
Introduction
Samuel sends Saul to destroy the Amalekites, and all their substance, 1Sam 15:1-3 . Saul collects an immense army and comes against their city, 1Sam 15:4 , 1Sam 15:5 . He desires the Kenites to remove from among the Amalekites, 1Sam 15:6 . He smites the Amalekites, and takes their king, Agag, prisoner, and saves the best of the spoil, 1Sam 15:7-9 . The Lord is displeased, and sends Samuel to reprove him, 1Sam 15:10 , 1Sam 15:11 . The conversation between Samuel and Saul, in which the latter endeavors to justify his conduct, 1Sam 15:12-23 . He is convinced that he has done wrong, and asks pardon, 1Sam 15:24-31 . Samuel causes Agag to be slain; for which he assigns the reasons, 1Sam 15:32-35 .
Verse 1
The Lord sent me to anoint thee - This gave him a right to say what immediately follows.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10091" type="x-p"/> I remember that which Amalek did - The Amalekites were a people of Arabia Petraea, who had occupied a tract of country on the frontiers of Egypt and Palestine. They had acted with great cruelty towards the Israelites on their coming out of Egypt. (See <reference osisRef="Exo.17.8">Exo 17:8</reference> (note), and the notes there). They came upon them when they were faint and weary, and smote the hindermost of the people - those who were too weak to keep up with the rest. (See <reference osisRef="Deu.25.18">Deu 25:18</reference>). And God then purposed that Amalek, as a nation, should be blotted out from under heaven; which purpose was now fulfilled by Saul upwards of four hundred years afterwards!

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10092" type="x-p"/> Slay both man and woman - Nothing could justify such an exterminating decree but the absolute authority of God. This was given: all the reasons of it we do not know; but this we know well, The Judge of all the earth doth right. This war was not for plunder, for God commanded that all the property as well as all the people should be destroyed.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10093" type="x-p"/> Two hundred thousand - and ten thousand - The Septuagint, in the London Polyglot, have Four Hundred thousand companies of Israel, and Thirty thousand companies of Judah. The Codex Alexandrinus has Ten thousand of each. The Complutensian Polyglot has Two Hundred thousand companies of Israel, and Ten thousand of Judah. And Josephus has Four Hundred thousand of Israel, and Thirty thousand of Judah. All the other versions are the same with the Hebrew text; and there is no difference in the MSS.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10095" type="x-p"/> Said unto the Kenites - The Kenites were an ancient people. entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen10096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10097" type="x-p"/> It repenteth me that I have set up Saul - That is, I placed him on the throne; I intended, if he had been obedient, to have established his kingdom. He has been disobedient; I change my purpose, and the kingdom shall not be established in his family. This is what is meant by God's repenting - changing a purpose according to conditions already laid down or mentally determined.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen10098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10099" type="x-p"/> The people spared the best of the sheep - It is very likely that the people did spare the best of the prey; and it is as likely that Saul might have restrained them if he would. That they might not love war, God had interdicted spoil and plunder, so the war was undertaken merely from a sense of duty, without any hope of enriching themselves by it.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen10102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10103" type="x-p"/> For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry - This is no translation of those difficult words, כי חטאת קסם מרי ואון ותרפים הפצר ki chattath kesem meri veaven utheraphim haphtsar. It appears to me that the three nouns which occur first in the text refer each to the three last in order. Thus, חטאת chattath, Transgression, refers to און aven, Iniquity, which is the principle whence transgression springs. קסם kesem, Divination, refers to תרפים teraphim, consecrated images or telesms, vulgarly talismans, used in incantations. And מרי meri, Rebellion, refers evidently to הפצר haphstar, Stubbornness, whence rebellion springs. The meaning therefore of this difficult place may be the following: As transgression comes from iniquity, divination from teraphim, and rebellion from stubbornness, so, because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king. All the versions are different.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen10114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10115" type="x-p"/> And Samuel came no more to see Saul - But we read, <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.22-1Sam.19.24">1Sam 19:22-24</reference>, that Saul went to see Samuel at Naioth, but this does not affect what is said here. From this time Samuel had no connection with Saul; he never more acknowledged him as king; he mourned and prayed for him, and continued to perform his prophetic functions at Ramah, and at Naioth, superintending the school of the prophets in that place.  <chapter eID="1Sam.15"/> <div eID="gen10115" type="x-p"/>

And Samuel came no more to see Saul - But we read, 1Sam 19:22-24 , that Saul went to see Samuel at Naioth, but this does not affect what is said here. From this time Samuel had no connection with Saul; he never more acknowledged him as king; he mourned and prayed for him, and continued to perform his prophetic functions at Ramah, and at Naioth, superintending the school of the prophets in that place.

Introduction
Samuel sends Saul to destroy the Amalekites, and all their substance, 1Sam 15:1-3 . Saul collects an immense army and comes against their city, 1Sam 15:4 , 1Sam 15:5 . He desires the Kenites to remove from among the Amalekites, 1Sam 15:6 . He smites the Amalekites, and takes their king, Agag, prisoner, and saves the best of the spoil, 1Sam 15:7-9 . The Lord is displeased, and sends Samuel to reprove him, 1Sam 15:10 , 1Sam 15:11 . The conversation between Samuel and Saul, in which the latter endeavors to justify his conduct, 1Sam 15:12-23 . He is convinced that he has done wrong, and asks pardon, 1Sam 15:24-31 . Samuel causes Agag to be slain; for which he assigns the reasons, 1Sam 15:32-35 .
